title: How to defend your sites from AI bots — David Mytton, Arcjet

primary.label: Security, Safety, Identity & Governance
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 99%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is defending websites from AI bots using layered security controls including IP reputation, fingerprinting, proof of work, and rate limiting. Security defense maps to the bot-mitigation and threat-modeling core; developer platforms applies because Arcjet is a security SDK for developers and open-source tools are demonstrated. All eight defense layers are presented for protecting live production websites against real automated traffic. The talk assumes web development familiarity but explains each technique from first principles, making it intermediate. This is a recorded conference presentation at AI Engineer. All evidence anchors are graded said_in_transcript and are drawn directly from the transcript.

summary: David Mytton, founder of Arcjet, presents on defending websites from AI bots, drawing on Arcjet's experience building a security SDK. The core problem is that nearly 50% of web traffic is now automated (up to 60% in gaming), imposing real costs: expensive serverless requests, bandwidth consumption, and potential denial of service. AI is making this demonstrably worse—Diaspora saw 24% of traffic from GPTBot, Read the Docs reduced bandwidth from 800GB to 200GB/day by blocking AI crawlers, and Wikipedia dedicates 35% of traffic to automated clients. Mytton frames a taxonomy of bots: traditionally "good" bots like Googlebot that provide search-indexing benefits, clearly "bad" scrapers, and a nuanced middle category of AI crawlers. OpenAI alone operates at least four bot types: a search crawler (beneficial), ChatGPT user (fetches URLs on behalf of real users), GPTBot (training, no direct benefit), and computer-use/operator bots that act as autonomous agents appearing as Chrome browsers. The talk walks through eight layered defenses. robots.txt is the starting point—voluntary, good bots follow it, bad bots may abuse it. User-agent strings are trivially spoofable but many bots honestly identify themselves. IP verification via reverse DNS confirms claimed crawler identity for major crawlers like Google, Bing, Apple, and OpenAI. IP reputation analysis examines data center vs residential origin, VPN/proxy usage, and geographic patterns, but residential proxy services can be purchased to bypass this, and geo data is notoriously inaccurate. CAPTCHAs are increasingly easy for AI to solve via LLMs or audio transcription. Proof of work requires computational effort before resource access—cheap for individuals but expensive for mass crawlers—though incentives matter: if a $200 ticket can be won, a few dollars of compute won't deter attackers. Difficulty can be scaled based on suspicion but introduces accessibility problems. Open source proof-of-work proxies like Anubis, Go Away, and Nepenthes exist. Emerging standards include Cloudflare's HTTP message signatures for cryptographic client verification and Apple's private access tokens (privacy pass) for iCloud subscribers, though both have limited adoption. Client fingerprinting using JA4 hash (TLS-level) and HTTP header analysis identifies clients across changing IP addresses, especially with IPv6. Rate limiting must be keyed on fingerprints or session IDs, not IP addresses alone, since IPs change constantly. Mytton concludes that robots.txt plus user-agent verification handles most sites' needs, but popular or high-value sites need the full layered stack.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Problem framing: automated traffic and costs
sections.summary: Mytton introduces the bot problem: nearly 50% of web traffic is automated (60% in gaming). Bots cause expensive requests (especially on serverless), bandwidth costs, and potential denial of service. AI is making this worse.

sections.title: Evidence that AI is worsening bot traffic
sections.summary: Examples of AI crawler impact: Diaspora saw 24% traffic from GPTBot, Read the Docs cut bandwidth from 800GB to 200GB/day by blocking AI crawlers, and Wikipedia spends 35% of traffic on automated clients. Scrapers make hundreds of thousands of requests without following rules.

sections.title: Bot taxonomy: good, bad, and AI crawlers
sections.summary: Historical distinction between good bots (Google search indexing, provides traffic benefit) and bad bots (scrapers). AI crawlers occupy a nuanced middle ground—training bots provide no direct benefit, but search-oriented AI bots are becoming a source of traffic and citations.

sections.title: OpenAI's four bot types
sections.summary: OpenAI operates at least four bot types: search bot (classic crawler, beneficial), ChatGPT user (fetches URLs on behalf of real users, nuanced), GPTBot (training, no direct benefit), and computer-use/operator bots (autonomous agents in VMs, appear as Chrome, challenging to detect).

sections.title: Defense layer 1: robots.txt
sections.summary: robots.txt lets site owners allow/disallow crawlers. It is entirely voluntary; good bots like Googlebot follow it, OpenAI mostly follows it, but problematic bots ignore it or use it to find disallowed content. Still a good starting point.

sections.title: Defense layer 2: User-Agent strings
sections.summary: Every request includes a User-Agent HTTP header. Many bots honestly identify themselves, and open source libraries (including Arcjet's database of thousands of user agents) can build rules. However, bad bots spoof this string, making it unreliable alone.

sections.title: Defense layer 3: IP verification via reverse DNS
sections.summary: Major crawlers (Apple, Bing, Google, OpenAI) support verification via reverse DNS lookup of source IP. Combining user-agent plus IP verification confirms claimed crawler identity.

sections.title: Defense layer 4: IP address reputation analysis
sections.summary: Analyze IP patterns: data center vs residential, VPN/proxy usage, country-level data. 12% of Cloudflare bot traffic came from AWS. Limitations include purchasable residential proxy services that make traffic appear from home ISPs, and notoriously inaccurate geo data due to satellite and 5G.

sections.title: Defense layer 5: CAPTCHAs and proof of work
sections.summary: CAPTCHAs have been used for decades but are increasingly easy for AI to solve via LLMs or audio transcription. Proof of work requires computational effort before resource access—cheap for individuals but expensive for mass crawlers. However, incentives matter: if profit from a successful attack exceeds compute cost, proof of work won't deter. Difficulty can scale based on suspicion but introduces accessibility problems.

sections.title: Open source proof-of-work tools
sections.summary: Open source projects like Anubis, Go Away, and Nepenthes implement proof-of-work proxies that can be installed on Kubernetes clusters or placed in front of applications to challenge suspicious users.

sections.title: Defense layer 6: HTTP message signatures and private access tokens
sections.summary: Emerging standards for cryptographic client verification. Cloudflare proposed HTTP message signatures where every request includes a cryptographic signature for automated clients—recently announced, still being developed. Apple announced private access tokens (privacy pass) allowing site owners to verify requests from iCloud subscribers via Safari, reducing CAPTCHAs, but adoption is limited outside the Apple ecosystem.

sections.title: Defense layer 7: Client fingerprinting
sections.summary: Fingerprinting generates a hash from network request characteristics to identify clients across changing IP addresses, especially with IPv6 where crawlers use banks of tens or hundreds of thousands of IPs. The open source JA4 hash is based on TLS fingerprinting; a proprietary version analyzes HTTP headers. Fingerprints enable blocking a single client regardless of IP count.

sections.title: Defense layer 8: Rate limiting with proper keying
sections.summary: Rate limiting works in conjunction with fingerprinting. Key insight: rate limiting on IP addresses is insufficient because IPs change constantly and malicious crawlers rotate them. Instead, key off user session IDs for logged-in users or JA4 hash fingerprints.

sections.title: Summary of all eight defenses and closing
sections.summary: Mytton recapitulates the eight defenses in order: robots.txt (starting point, voluntary), user-agent analysis with verification (handles most sites' needs), IP reputation, proof of work, experimental HTTP signatures, and fingerprinting combined with rate limits (where most advanced sites land). High-value or popular sites need the full stack. A detailed writeup is available at blog.arcjet.com.

Open source proof-of-work proxies: Anubis, Go Away, and Nepenthes deployable on Kubernetes
